t: LeetCode 2203 - Minimum Weighted Subgraph With the Required Paths: Three Dijkstras and a Meeting Point
o: **Understanding the problem.** Among all subgraphs of a weighted directed graph in which both src1 and src2 can reach dest, we must return the one whose edge weights sum smallest, or -1 if none exists. In Example 1 (n = 6, src1 = 0, src2 = 1, dest = 5) the answer is 9: taking edges 1->0 (3) and 0->5 (6) lets both sources reach node 5, and no cheaper selection exists. The crucial structural observation is that any feasible subgraph contains a src1-to-dest path and a src2-to-dest path, which share at least the endpoint dest; picking a common node v on their overlap splits the requirement into d(src1, v) + d(src2, v) + d(v, dest). Conversely, the union of those three shortest paths is itself feasible, so the answer is the minimum of this expression over all nodes v. Since n and the edge count reach 100000 and weights reach 100000, we need roughly linear time, and positive weights make Dijkstra the tool of choice; total weights can exceed 32-bit range, so 64-bit sums are mandatory.
k: Any feasible subgraph contains walks src1 -> v, src2 -> v and v -> dest for some meeting node v, so its weight is at least d(src1, v) + d(src2, v) + d(v, dest).
The union of the three shortest paths realizing that minimum is itself a feasible subgraph, so sweeping v over all nodes yields the exact optimum.
d(v, dest) for every v is one Dijkstra run away: run it on the reversed graph from dest.
Distances reach about 10^10, so C++/Java need long/long long accumulators.

a.n: Approach 1: Try Every Meeting Node (Brute Force)
a.i: Guess the meeting node v directly: for each candidate, run Dijkstra from src1 stopping at v, from src2 stopping at v, and from v stopping at dest, then sum the three distances. Recomputing nearly identical searches n times is wasteful, but it isolates the decomposition that the optimal solution exploits.
s: For each node v, run three early-exiting Dijkstra searches: src1 -> v, src2 -> v, v -> dest.
Skip candidates with an unreachable leg; otherwise compare the sum against the best.
Return the minimum, or -1 if every candidate had an infinite leg.
a.t: O(n * m log n) - each of n candidate meeting nodes triggers up to three Dijkstra runs over m edges
a.sp: O(n + m) - adjacency list plus distance array and heap

a.n: Approach 2: Three Dijkstra Runs Plus One Sweep (Optimal)
a.i: The brute force redoes identical work: the shortest-path distances out of src1 do not depend on the guessed meeting node, and neither do those out of src2. Even better, dist(v, dest) for all v simultaneously is exactly one Dijkstra run from dest on the reversed graph. Compute the three full distance arrays once, then evaluate d1[v] + d2[v] + d3[v] in a single linear sweep.
s: Build forward and reversed adjacency lists.
Run Dijkstra from src1 and from src2 on the forward graph, giving d1 and d2.
Run Dijkstra from dest on the reversed graph, giving d3.
Return min over v of d1[v] + d2[v] + d3[v], or -1 if that minimum involves an infinite distance.
a.t: O(m log n) - three heap-based Dijkstra runs dominate (m = number of edges)
a.sp: O(n + m) - forward and reversed adjacency lists plus three distance arrays

w: In an interview, state the meeting-point decomposition first - it converts an unfamiliar subgraph-selection problem into three standard shortest-path computations, and the sweep proves optimality in one line. Pitfalls: forgetting that the dest leg requires reversing every edge; summing distances with 32-bit integers (weights up to 10^5 over 10^5 edges overflow); returning -1 whenever any single node lacks a finite triple rather than only when no node has one. A node with an infinite d1, d2 or d3 is simply skipped. Likely follow-ups: several destination nodes (run one multi-source Dijkstra on the reversed graph), or reconstructing the actual edge set (keep parent pointers from each run).
